design_detail: Cross-sectional PET study. Striatal dopamine transporter (DAT) availability measured with [11C]d-threo-methylphenidate in 15 people with methamphetamine dependence (abstinent at least 2 weeks) and 18 non-using controls. A neuropsychological battery was given to the methamphetamine group only; DAT was correlated with test scores within that group.
can_establish: That this group of abstinent heavy users had lower striatal DAT availability than this control group, and that within the user group lower DAT went with slower motor tasks and fewer words recalled.
cannot_establish: That methamphetamine caused the lower DAT (no pre-use scan); that it reflects loss of dopamine terminals rather than down-regulation (the authors say this is unknown, p. 381); that users were cognitively impaired compared with controls or norms (controls were not tested); or whether DAT recovers (single time point).

sample.recruitment: Users from drug rehabilitation centres in the Los Angeles area; controls by local advertisement (p. 378).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Users: DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence; average use of at least 0.5 g/day, at least 5 days a week, for at least 2 years; at least 2 weeks' abstinence confirmed by urine toxicology. Both groups excluded for HIV seropositivity (tested in users only), comorbid psychiatric or neurological disorder, medical illness, dependence on drugs other than methamphetamine or nicotine, and head trauma (p. 378).
sample.demographics: Users: 6 men, 9 women; mean age 32 (SD 7); estimated verbal IQ (NART-R) 100 (SD 9). Controls: 12 men, 6 women; mean age 31 (SD 7); estimated IQ 107 (SD 10) (pp. 377–378). Education not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Treatment-centre sample of heavy, long-term users (mean 11 years of use) against advertisement-recruited controls. Groups differ in sex ratio (60% vs 33% women) and estimated IQ (100 vs 107); neither is adjusted for. Smoking is not reported in this paper, though the authors note most users smoke (p. 381); the companion paper on the same users reports 73% smokers vs 24% of controls (Volkow, Chang, Wang, Fowler, Franceschi, et al., 2001c, p. 387).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported drug-use history corroborated by two physicians; abstinence confirmed by urine toxicology (p. 378).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported. Duration mean 11 years (SD 6). Average daily amount mean 1.6 g (SD 3.0, range 0.3–10.0). Cumulative amount mean 12,290 g (range 514–86,400). Route: smoking and snorting 11 (73%), injection and snorting 2 (13%), smoking only 2 (13%) (Table 1, p. 378).
exposure.polysubstance: Dependence on any other drug except nicotine excluded; use of other drugs short of dependence (alcohol, cannabis) was not quantified (p. 378).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 2 weeks, urine-confirmed. Mean 5.9 months since last use (SD 9.0, range 0.5–36); 12 users within 6 months, 3 users 11–36 months (pp. 378–379).

comparison.controls: 18 healthy volunteers with no history of drug abuse, recruited by advertisement (p. 378).
comparison.matching: Similar mean age. Not matched on sex or estimated IQ; education and smoking not reported.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use DAT or cognitive measurement. Premorbid ability only as a current reading-test estimate, which was lower in users.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: History of drug problems excluded; controls' alcohol and nicotine use not reported.

outcomes.instruments: PET with [11C]d-threo-methylphenidate; DAT availability as Bmax/Kd from the striatum-to-cerebellum distribution-volume ratio (graphical analysis) (p. 378). Neuropsychological battery, users only: Timed Gait, Grooved Pegboard, California Computerized Assessment Package, Symbol Digit Modalities, Trail Making, Stroop, Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (immediate, delayed, interference recall), CES-D, NART-R (p. 378).
outcomes.validity_norms: Neuropsychological scores were compared neither with controls nor with published norms.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Impairment' was operationalized only as a within-user correlation between DAT and test scores. No group comparison and no normative comparison (pp. 379–380).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial: 5 a priori correlations (2 motor tasks, 3 recall scores) at p<0.05; 7 exploratory correlations at p<0.007 (p. 379). Correlations of DAT with years of use, dose and days since last use were not corrected.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported for region-of-interest drawing or testing.

analysis.effect_sizes: DAT availability (Bmax/Kd), users vs controls: caudate 1.3 (SD 0.2) vs 1.8 (SD 0.3), 27.8% lower; putamen 1.5 (SD 0.2) vs 1.9 (SD 0.2), 21.1% lower; t>4.7, df=31, p<0.0001 (Table 2, p. 379). Editors' calculation from Table 2: standardized differences of about 1.9 (caudate) and 2.0 (putamen), approximate because means and SDs are printed to one decimal. Individual values overlap between groups: several users lie within the control range in both regions (Figure 2, p. 379). Within users, striatal DAT correlated with Timed Gait r=0.53, Grooved Pegboard r=0.57, AVLT interference recall r=0.70, delayed recall r=0.64, immediate recall r=0.58; exploratory Trail Making r=0.61 (pp. 379–380). DAT and years of use: caudate r=0.54; no correlation with dose (r<0.37) or days since last use (r<0.11) (p. 379).
analysis.covariates: None. Unadjusted t-tests and Pearson correlations.
analysis.selective_reporting: Group means for the neuropsychological tests are not reported, and the users' scores are not compared with controls or norms, although the abstract says DAT reduction 'was associated with motor slowing and memory impairment'.
analysis.power: Not reported. With n=15, a correlation of r=0.53 has a 95% interval of roughly 0.02 to 0.82 (editors' calculation, Fisher z).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Lower striatal DAT availability in 15 abstinent heavy users than in 18 controls, with overlapping individual values; within users, lower DAT went with slower motor tasks and fewer words recalled.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion say methamphetamine at the doses people use leads to DAT reduction associated with motor and cognitive impairment, and call for urgently warning the public of its damaging effects on the brain (abstract, p. 377; p. 381). The discussion concedes it is unknown whether the reduction reflects damage to dopamine terminals or down-regulation of the transporter (p. 381). No comparison with controls or norms supports the word 'impairment'. The inference that DAT does not recover significantly after a year (p. 381) rests on a null correlation with time since last use in 15 people, only 3 of them abstinent longer than 11 months; the same group's follow-up found significant DAT increases with protracted abstinence (Volkow, Chang, Wang, Fowler, Franceschi, et al., 2001b).

timeline.event: Same users scanned with FDG: higher global metabolism, lower relative striatal and thalamic metabolism; the paper states neuropsychological tests were given to users only
Follow-up of 5 users who stayed abstinent: DAT rose 19% (caudate) and 16% (putamen); this contradicts the no-recovery inference
Thalamic but not striatal metabolism partly recovered with protracted abstinence in the same programme
Critical review: the paper reports no cognitive comparison with controls and no educational data; the clinical meaning of the DAT difference is unknown
Critical assessment of whether the DAT findings in users indicate neuronal damage (to be appraised from the full text)

replication.where_it_stands: Lower striatal DAT availability in heavy users compared with non-users has been reported by several PET groups (McCann et al., 1998; Sekine et al., 2001; Johanson et al., 2006; McCann et al., 2008, as summarized by Hart et al., 2012, pp. 592–596; primary papers to be appraised). Its meaning (loss of terminals vs regulation), its reversibility and its functional consequence remain the open questions.

funding.funder: US Department of Energy contract (Brookhaven National Laboratory); National Institute on Drug Abuse grants; Office of National Drug Control Policy; NIH General Clinical Research Center grant (p. 381).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: The Office of National Drug Control Policy is the US federal drug-policy office. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Longitudinal PET in people before and after starting regular use, with matched non-using comparison participants scanned at the same intervals; or post-mortem measurement of DAT together with a stable terminal marker (VMAT2) in the same brains; with cognitive testing of both groups against norms.

domains.note: No adjustment. Groups differ in sex ratio, estimated IQ and (per the companion paper) smoking; other drug use not quantified; premorbid DAT unknown.
Dependence diagnosis is reliable; amounts are self-reported and the printed dose range contradicts the inclusion criterion.
Treatment-centre heavy users vs advertisement-recruited controls.
Abstinence ranged from 2 weeks to 3 years; if DAT changes with abstinence, the group difference depends on when people were scanned.
PET quantification is objective, but regions were drawn by hand and blinding to group is not reported.
Cognitive results are reported only as within-user correlations; group means and normative comparison are absent.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The DAT group difference is large and objectively measured, but it cannot be attributed to methamphetamine because of uncontrolled confounding and selection; the cognitive conclusions rest on correlations within 15 users without any comparison group.

key_findings.finding: Striatal DAT availability was 27.8% lower in the caudate and 21.1% lower in the putamen in 15 abstinent users than in 18 controls (Bmax/Kd 1.3 vs 1.8 and 1.5 vs 1.9).
Individual DAT values overlap between groups: several users fall within the control range in both caudate and putamen.
Three users abstinent 11–36 months still had lower DAT than the control mean.
key_findings.note: Read from Figures 2 and 3 (approximate): the caudate values of these three users (about 1.35–1.43) lie within the control range (lowest control about 1.3); their putamen values (about 1.48–1.61) are at or just below the bottom of the control range (about 1.57).

key_findings.finding: Within users, lower striatal DAT correlated with slower Timed Gait (r=0.53) and Grooved Pegboard (r=0.57) and with fewer words recalled on the AVLT (r=0.58–0.70); n=15.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd (last) paragraph (p. 379, right column, continuing on p. 380); Figure 4 (p. 380)

key_findings.finding: Neuropsychological tests were given to the methamphetamine group only; no comparison with controls or norms is reported.
key_findings.note: Confirmed explicitly in the companion paper (Volkow et al., 2001c, p. 387).

key_findings.finding: DAT was not correlated with self-reported dose (r<0.37) or with days since last use (r<0.11); caudate DAT correlated with years of use (r=0.54, direction not printed).
The authors state it is unknown whether the DAT reduction reflects terminal damage or down-regulation of the transporter.

The authors note that the reduction was of similar size in the caudate and putamen (27.8% and 21.1%), unlike Parkinson's disease, in which the putamen is more often affected than the caudate, and take this to suggest a different mechanism; no people with Parkinson's disease were studied.

reporting_issues.issue: The inclusion criterion of at least 0.5 g/day (p. 378) is contradicted by Table 1, where average daily dose ranges from 0.3 g.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the criterion was not applied strictly or the table reports a different quantity. The follow-up paper from the same programme states a criterion of 0.25 g/day (Volkow et al., 2001b, p. 9415).

reporting_issues.issue: All correlations are printed without signs (for example Timed Gait r=0.53, where lower DAT is described as going with slower times, a negative relation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Direction has to be inferred from the text and Figure 4; for years of use (r=0.54) the direction is not stated at all.

reporting_issues.issue: Correlations with n=15 are reported with df=14; the expected value is n−2=13.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; p-values would be marginally larger.

reporting_issues.issue: No check of the robustness of the within-user correlations is reported, although the participant with the lowest striatal DAT (about 1.0, read from Figure 4) lies at the low end of the fitted line in all four panels.
reporting_issues.consequence: With n=15 the correlations may depend substantially on this one participant; their size is less certain than the printed r values suggest.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that three users had DAT levels within the range of low-severity Parkinson's disease, and the suggestion that they had no extrapyramidal symptoms because they could still compensate, come without these users' values or any reported assessment of motor signs.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Parkinson's comparison, and the later-life parkinsonism risk the discussion raises, cannot be checked from the paper.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 377–382 (all pages; figures checked on the rendered page)

disagreements.reviewer: Confirmed, with an optional precision: the three long-abstinent users are below the control means, but their caudate values (about 1.35–1.43) lie within the control range (lowest control about 1.3) (Figure 3 vs Figure 2, p. 379).
disagreements.resolution: Checked on 300-dpi crops of Figures 2 and 3 (p. 379): caudate about 1.43, 1.42 and 1.35 against a lowest control of about 1.28; putamen about 1.61, 1.48 and 1.48 against a lowest control of about 1.57. Added as a note because the abstract rests its 'evident even after 11 months' statement on these three people.

disagreements.reviewer: Wrong location: Results has only two paragraphs; the correlations are in the 2nd (last), p. 379 right column continuing on p. 380; Figure 4 is on p. 380.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on the rendered pp. 379–380: the Results section has two paragraphs and the DAT–test correlations are in the second. Data unchanged.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed: the authors note the reduction was similar in caudate and putamen, unlike Parkinson's disease, and infer a different mechanism (p. 380, Discussion, right column).
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on p. 380. Added as a key finding because the claim on the Parkinson's pattern (cl_meth_dopamine_damage) anchors it; worded as the authors' interpretation, since the comparison with Parkinson's disease comes from the literature, not from this study's data.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed: one participant with the lowest DAT (about 1.0) sits at the extreme of all four panels of Figure 4; with n=15 and no robustness check, the correlations may depend heavily on that participant.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on a 300-dpi crop of Figure 4: the lowest-DAT point lies at the lower end of each fitted line (Timed Gait about 11.6 s, Pegboard about 85 s, interference recall 7 words, delayed recall 5 words). No sensitivity analysis is reported. Added as a reporting issue; the consequence is worded as a possibility, since the data are not available to quantify the influence.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed: the authors state that three users had DAT within the range reported for mild Parkinson's disease without showing those values or extrapyramidal assessments (p. 380).
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on p. 380 (Discussion, right column, top): no values, no identification of the three users and no extrapyramidal rating are reported. Added as a reporting issue.
